# Ventriloquist

> Turn a Mac app into an MCP server using the macOS accessibility API. An agent
> explores the app once, the useful actions are compiled into a JSON "pack" of
> typed tools, and after that every call is a deterministic replay that takes
> milliseconds and never touches a model. No screenshots, no vision, no pixel
> coordinates anywhere in the codebase.

This file is the whole project explained in one place, written for both people
and language models. The repo is https://github.com/ShaanGS/ventriloquist. The
package is `vent`, the CLI is `vent`, the language is Python 3.11+, macOS only.

## The idea in one paragraph

Computer-use agents today are interpreters: a model looks at the screen and
decides every click, every time, which is slow, expensive, and flaky.
Ventriloquist is the compiler version. You pay the model cost once, during a
guarded exploration of the app's accessibility tree. What comes out is a pack
of typed tools like `write_document(text)` or `search_workspace(query)`, each
backed by recorded accessibility actions with durable element anchors. Serving
those tools over MCP requires no model, no network, and no vision. When an app
update breaks a recorded anchor, a model is brought back for one job only:
re-ground the anchor. The fix is quarantined and nothing changes on disk until
a human approves it through `vent verify`.

## Why the accessibility tree

Every Mac app has shipped an accessibility (AX) tree for decades because
screen readers depend on it. It gives you semantic elements (buttons, text
areas, rows) with roles, labels, and real actions (press, set value), which is
a far better contract than pixels. The whole system stands on it: reading the
tree (never the screen), acting through AX actions (never synthetic mouse
events), and verifying through live re-reads of element values.

## Architecture, component by component

Everything lives in the `vent/` package. One file per concern:

- `ax.py`. The only file that talks to the macOS accessibility C API
  (via pyobjc). Elements, attributes, actions, app discovery, activation,
  trust checks, screen-lock detection. Imports are guarded so the test suite
  runs on Linux.
- `snapshot.py`. Walks an app's tree into a semantic snapshot: a flat list of
  surfaced nodes, each with role, subrole, label, identifier, value preview,
  available actions, and its full ancestor chain. Skips the menu bar by
  default. Guards against cyclic trees (real apps have returned an element as
  its own child). One shared depth limit, `MAX_TREE_DEPTH = 50`, used by both
  snapshots and anchor resolution so an anchor minted from an inspect can
  always be reached by the resolver. It was 25 until VS Code proved Chromium
  trees run deeper.
- `anchors.py`. The heart of durability. An anchor records how to find an
  element again later: role, identifier, every label it has been observed
  under, window title, and the full ancestor chain with ordinals. Resolution
  walks the live tree, scores every candidate (identifier outranks label,
  chain similarity and position matter, wrong window is a penalty), and
  refuses to answer if the best two candidates score too close together.
  Refusing to guess is a feature: a wrong binding is the worst outcome, a
  refusal just means re-record or heal.
- `packs.py`. The pack format. A pack is one JSON file per app bundle id under
  `packs/`, containing typed tools. Each tool has a name, description, risk
  level (`read_only`, `mutating`, `high`), parameter schema, preconditions,
  steps, and verify checks. Steps use a closed op set: `press`, `set_value`,
  `pick`, `reveal`, `raise_window`, `open_app`, `wait_for`, `read_value`.
  There is deliberately no exec, no shell, no AppleScript, no arbitrary code.
  Loading validates everything and rejects unknown ops or risks. Saves are
  atomic (temp file plus rename).
- `runtime.py`. Deterministic replay. For each step: resolve the anchor,
  assert the expected role, perform the action, then wait for the tree to
  settle (a shape-hash poll that distinguishes "reacted then went quiet" from
  "nothing happened"). Verify checks re-read live element values, never
  snapshot previews. Two Chromium-specific pumps live here: after any mutating
  op the runtime performs a no-op scroll-to-visible on the element, because
  Chromium hosts publish their accessibility tree lazily and reads would
  otherwise return the pre-action tree forever; and `wait_for` performs the
  same nudge between polls. `runtime.py` never imports `llm.py`.
- `server.py`. The MCP stdio server. Loads every pack, exposes each tool as
  `<app>_<tool>`, serializes calls with per-app locks (a GUI is one global
  mutable resource), and refuses `high` risk tools unless the process was
  started with `VENT_ALLOW_HIGH=1`. Never imports `llm.py` either.
- `harness.py`. Durability measurement. Records anchors for an app's
  elements, perturbs the app (real window resize, optionally a full quit and
  relaunch), and re-resolves everything. Survival only counts when the found
  element is provably the recorded one; lookalikes count as WRONG, and the
  design goal is zero wrong. Skips rounds honestly when the screen is locked
  or the app never comes back.
- `explorer.py`. The model-driven part of compile time. The model nominates
  elements worth probing; the policy screens every nomination; only reversible
  or budgeted actions execute (a probe writes into an empty field and restores
  the prior value immediately). Everything that ran is recorded into a trace.
- `policy.py`. The safety screen, applied after the model. Closed action
  space, destructive-word detection, per-session budgets for cumulative
  actions like New Note, secure fields stripped before anything sees them.
- `compiler.py`. Turns a trace into proposed tools. Composes only actions that
  actually executed. Every proposal is shown to a human two ways: the model's
  description, and a deterministic summary built from the literal recorded
  steps. The steps are ground truth; the description is not. Nothing is
  written without approval. Known limitation: compiling writes the whole pack
  file, it does not merge into an existing one.
- `heal.py`. When resolution fails at runtime with healing enabled, the model
  gets the broken anchor plus a fresh snapshot and proposes a re-grounding.
  It refuses truncated snapshots, cross-role targets, and destructive
  targets. The fix goes into the pack's `healed_pending` quarantine, is
  usable for the current call, and is only promoted into the anchor of record
  when a human approves it in `vent verify`.
- `llm.py`. The single home for every model call, and the only file with
  network egress. Two backends, tried in order: the Anthropic SDK (needs
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or an `ant auth login` profile, uses the API's
  structured output so responses are schema-guaranteed), and the Claude Code
  CLI (`claude -p`, print mode, tools disabled, works with a subscription
  login and no API key; the schema travels in the prompt and responses are
  parsed strictly, with exactly one wrapping markdown fence tolerated as
  transport framing). App-derived text is wrapped in nonce-delimited
  untrusted-content markers before it reaches a prompt.
- `cli.py`. Click-based CLI wiring all of the above together.

## The pack format, concretely

```json
{
  "format_version": 2,
  "bundle_id": "com.apple.TextEdit",
  "app_name": "TextEdit",
  "app_version": "1.19",
  "tools": [
    {
      "name": "write_document",
      "description": "Replace the entire text of the frontmost document.",
      "risk": "mutating",
      "params": {"text": {"type": "string", "description": "New content."}},
      "preconditions": [{"kind": "window_exists"}],
      "steps": [
        {
          "op": "set_value",
          "anchor": {
            "role": "AXTextArea",
            "identifier": "First Text View",
            "labels": [],
            "window_title": "vent-demo.txt",
            "chain": [
              {"role": "AXApplication", "label": "TextEdit", "ordinal": 0, "index": 0},
              {"role": "AXWindow", "identifier": "_NS:34", "ordinal": 0, "index": 0},
              {"role": "AXScrollArea", "identifier": "_NS:8", "ordinal": 0, "index": 0},
              {"role": "AXTextArea", "identifier": "First Text View", "ordinal": 0, "index": 0}
            ]
          },
          "value": {"param": "text"},
          "expect": {"role": "AXTextArea"}
        }
      ],
      "verify": [
        {"kind": "value_contains", "anchor": {"...": "same anchor"}, "param": "text"}
      ]
    }
  ],
  "healed_pending": []
}
```

Verify kinds are `value_equals`, `value_contains` (against a param or a
literal), and `element_exists`. Preconditions are `app_running` and
`window_exists`. `wait_for` steps take a `timeout_s` and poll until the
anchor resolves. Anchors remember every label they have been observed under,
which is how a pack survived VS Code renaming its sidebar headings from
"SOURCE CONTROL" to "Source Control" in an update.

## The CLI

```
vent doctor [APP]      check Accessibility permission, probe an app's tree health
vent apps              list running apps vent can attach to
vent inspect APP       print the semantic snapshot (node ids, roles, labels, actions)
vent anchor APP NODE   print the durable anchor for a node, for hand-authoring packs
vent explore APP       model probes under the policy, records a trace (--no-values redacts field content)
vent compile APP       propose tools from the trace, human approves each against literal steps
vent run APP TOOL      execute one compiled tool directly (--arg key=value, --heal to enable re-grounding)
vent serve             serve every pack as MCP tools over stdio
vent verify APP        dry-resolve every anchor, report durability, offer to promote quarantined heals
vent harness APP       measure anchor durability under resize (--restart adds quit and relaunch)
```

Wiring into Claude Code: `claude mcp add ventriloquist -- /path/to/.venv/bin/vent serve`.
Tools appear as `textedit_write_document` and so on.

## Security model, condensed

The full threat model is docs/SECURITY.md (threats T1 through T10). The load
bearing invariants:

- Closed action space. No op runs code, shell commands, or AppleScript.
  Adding an op is a breaking change to the threat model.
- The model composes but never authors. Tools are built only from actions
  that actually executed under the policy; model output is parsed against a
  JSON schema and rejected on any mismatch, never repaired.
- Policy screens after the model, so a prompt-injected model still cannot
  reach anything the policy refuses.
- `runtime.py` and `server.py` never import `llm.py`. Serving packs cannot
  make a model call, structurally.
- Healed anchors are quarantined, never silently promoted.
- App-derived text (labels, values, titles) is treated as attacker-influenced
  and wrapped in nonce-delimited markers before any prompt.
- Secure fields are dropped before anything can see or target them.
- Snapshots sent to a model are scrubbed; `--no-values` replaces every field
  value with a length marker so exploration can run without field content
  leaving the machine.
- All network egress lives in one file, `llm.py`.
- High risk tools are refused by the server unless it was started with
  `VENT_ALLOW_HIGH=1`, an operator decision, never a caller decision.

Honest limits, also documented: probe reversibility is local (an app that
syncs on every keystroke may transmit a probe string before the restore), and
truncation of previews is a privacy measure, not an injection defense.

## Durability numbers (this machine, macOS 26)

```
TextEdit: baseline 100%,  resized 100%,   0 wrong
Finder:   baseline 100%,  resized 100%,   0 wrong
VS Code:  baseline  95%,  resized  87.5%, restart 92.5%, 0 wrong  (40 anchors)
```

The VS Code restart round is a full quit and relaunch; 37 of 40 anchors still
bind to provably the same element. Non-survivors are ambiguity refusals, not
wrong bindings. The VS Code pack's own curated anchors went 6 for 6 across
view switches, a resize, and a real app update.

## Hard-won platform knowledge (mostly Electron)

- Chromium trees are deep. The old depth budget of 25 could not reach VS
  Code's search box; the shared limit is now 50.
- Chromium publishes its accessibility tree lazily. After an action, reads
  return the pre-action tree until the next action arrives, however long you
  poll. The runtime pumps a no-op scroll-to-visible after mutating ops and
  between `wait_for` polls.
- The cached AXValue of Chromium radio buttons is unreliable. Verify view
  switches by waiting for the view's content to exist, not by reading the
  pressed control's value.
- VS Code must be launched with `--force-renderer-accessibility`. The
  AXManualAccessibility request alone produces a tree that reads fine but
  silently ignores every action.
- VS Code's process name is `Code` but its AppleScript name is
  `Visual Studio Code`; activating "Code" fails silently.
- A locked screen makes every app serve an empty tree while the permission
  check still passes. `vent doctor` names this state.
- Apps relaunched from a background process serve degraded menubar-only trees
  until genuinely foregrounded.
- NSWorkspace's running-application list is KVO-maintained and freezes in a
  process that never pumps the run loop; `ax.running_apps` pumps briefly on
  every read.
- macOS AX trees can be cyclic; every walk carries an ancestor-path cycle
  guard.
- An in-place app auto-update can wedge an Electron app's AX bridge until a
  full quit and relaunch.

## Development story and quality bar

Built phase by phase, each phase getting an adversarial code review and a
separate security review before the next began, with findings fixed in
follow-up commits. 91 offline tests run in CI on Linux and macOS; the tests
use fake element trees and a scripted-model seam
(`llm.set_completer_for_tests`) so no test needs macOS, credentials, or
network. Every model-driven path has also been validated live: exploration,
compilation with the human gate (which caught a genuinely bad tool proposal),
and the full break, heal, quarantine, promote cycle.

## Files worth reading, in order

1. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md   the design, section by section
2. docs/SECURITY.md       the threat model, T1 through T10
3. docs/HANDOFF.md        current state, findings, and gotchas
4. vent/anchors.py        scoring and refusal, the durability core
5. vent/runtime.py        replay, settle, verify, the Chromium pumps
6. packs/                 real packs for TextEdit and VS Code
